1:
Henry places the altar first: God manifested his presence in the tabernacle, which only the priests entered as his domestic servants, while the people attended outside as common subjects in the court, bringing sacrifices to an altar that sanctified their gifts; and as the oracles came out to them from the mercy-seat, a communion was settled between God and Israel. Wesley reproduces the sentences almost unaltered.

An altar of wood sits awkwardly beside the earlier command that altars be of earth or unhewn stone, and Ellicott and Keil resolve it the same way independently. Ellicott adopts what he calls the probably correct explanation of the Jewish commentators: what is directed here is an altar-case rather than an altar, the true altar being the earth with which the bronze-plated case was filled at each halt. Keil, reasoning from Exodus 20, arrives at the same construction: the framework was filled with earth, or gravel and stones, whenever the altar was used, the whole levelled to form a hearth — which let it be carried and pitched anywhere and kept the wooden walls from burning.

Whether horned altars were peculiar to Israel produces a head-on collision, and both sides bring evidence. Ellicott denies the common claim flatly, naming Kalisch as its author, and asserts that horns were so far as is known peculiar to Israelite altars. Clarke had said the opposite and gone looking for proof: horns were much used on heathen altars, some built entirely of the horns of sacrificed beasts, and he lists the coin reverses on which horned altars appear — of Antoninus, Faustina, Valerian and others. On what the horns were for the two agree more than they differ. Clarke gives three uses — ornament, keeping the carcass from falling, binding the victim; Wesley names two; Ellicott traces a development, that they began as mere ornaments at the four upper corners but came to be thought essential, the virtue of the altar being supposed to lie especially in them, so that victims were bound to them, criminals clung to them, and the blood of sin offerings was smeared on them. Gill reads them as the power of Christ, the horn of salvation, their standing at four corners answering to the four quarters of the world.

Gill's contribution is wholly negative. This altar, he insists, was not typical of the altar of the heart, since the heart is not brass to bear the fire of divine wrath and does not sanctify the gift, being itself impure; nor of the Lord's table, which is a table and not an altar, a feast and not a sacrifice, neither greater than the gift nor sanctifying it. Calvin builds the positive type instead, from the name of the burnt offering, whose root means mounting upward: the Israelites were reminded that they needed purifying in order to ascend to God. He observes that burnt sacrifices existed from the beginning of the human race, before any written law, by the secret inspiration of God's Spirit, and reads the burning as teaching that flesh must be consumed by the Spirit — so that under this type they acknowledged that the flesh of Christ must receive as much from the divine power, the Apostle testifying that he offered himself through the Spirit.

Where the grating stood nobody can settle. Ellicott states two views and declines between them: that it reached from mid-altar to the base and protected the sides from the priests' feet, or that it surrounded the upper part and caught pieces of the victims that fell — there being, he says, no sufficient data to decide. On the dimensions Clarke does the arithmetic, reckoning the cubit at twenty-one inches to give an altar eight feet nine inches square and five feet three high; Ellicott explains the modest height practically, that a greater one would have made it hard to arrange the victims.
6:
Whether the altar was genuinely hollow or filled is the substance of this short passage, and Gill takes the opposite side from the reconstruction the others favour. The frame being of boards, he says, there was nothing inside but the grate let down into the middle of the square, which made it light to carry; and he then names and rejects the alternative — the Targum of Jonathan and other Jewish writers represent the hollow as filled up with dust and earth so as to answer the altar of earth Moses had earlier been bidden to make, but this seems to him quite contrary to the present direction. Clarke agrees with him without argument: a kind of framework with nothing solid inside, covered only by the grating at the top, which rendered it more light and portable. Keil, expounding the same clause, takes the filling for granted.

Gill then makes the hollowness itself the type, and it is the only reading of it offered here: the emptiness of the altar may denote the emptiness of Christ when he became a sacrifice, who emptied himself as it were of all his greatness, glory and riches when he became incarnate, and became mean and poor for his people's sake, that through his poverty they might be made rich.

The rings the staves passed through are also disputed, and Gill sets out the alternatives before choosing. Some, including Jarchi, put the staves into the rings of the grate. Dr. Lightfoot supposed those rings came out through the altar frame at each corner and hung clear of it, so that the staves passing through them fastened frame and grate together and the two were carried as one. Gill prefers a simpler arrangement: the grate had rings of its own, by which it was lowered and lifted and carried under a purple cloth, and the altar had its own rings on its sides, into which these staves were put. Keil states only what the text states, that the staves were to be put into the rings and to lie along the two sides for carrying, and that the poles were of acacia-wood covered with brass. Ellicott's notes here do nothing but refer the reader back to his own earlier comments.
9:
What the court typifies divides the two who make most of it. Henry takes it for the church, enclosed and distinguished from the world, its stability figured by the pillars and its clothing by the clean linen that is the righteousness of saints; and he ends with a release, that this court would contain but few worshippers, whereas now under the gospel the enclosure is taken down, God's will being that men pray everywhere, so there is room for all. Wesley reproduces the passage almost entire, down to the closing thanks. Gill draws the opposite lesson from the same enclosure: it typifies the visible church on earth, which though separated from the world consists of professors good and bad, real saints and hypocrites — precisely because Israelites of every character, sex and state entered this court. Calvin takes it as the court of the people, distinct from the priests', where they consecrated their victims, offered prayers and were reconciled; and he finds the condition of mankind shown in the arrangement, since they were forbidden the sanctuary and yet reminded that men, unworthy outcasts as they are, are received by God if they seek him simply and with due humility.

The material of the pillars is disputed, and Gill lays out three answers before choosing. Philo made them of cedar; most take them for shittim wood; but the plain and express words of the text make them, like their sockets, of brass, and Josephus says so expressly — which Gill thinks fittest for the purpose. Ellicott has the same fight on his hands with a modern: Kalisch says the pillars of the court were of wood and not plated with metal, and Ellicott answers that this passage and another, rightly translated, contradict him. Gill also reasons from the spacing, that twenty pillars carrying a hundred cubits of hangings must have stood five cubits apart, and reads the pillars as figuring the ministers of the gospel, who are the principal support of the churches and are set for the defence of it.

Ellicott corrects three renderings in passing. The hangings are named by a new and rare word which the Greek version turns into sails, and he takes it for a coarse sail-cloth woven with interstices, through which what went on inside the court might be seen — a point Clarke reaches from the other direction by observing that the enclosure was only half the height of the tabernacle, so that the sacred building might easily be seen by the people from without. Fine twined linen he takes to mean linen thread of several strands, not fine linen in the modern sense. And the fillets are rather connecting-rods, uniting the pillars and helping to support the hangings; Keil agrees and draws a distinction from it, that the court's rods were silver while those at the dwelling's entrance were wood overlaid with gold, so the two must have served different purposes, these being simply rods to fasten hangings to.

On the dimensions Clarke and Henry differ in their arithmetic more than in their cubits. Henry, with Wesley after him, reckons the court fifty yards by twenty-five; Clarke makes the hundred cubits about fifty-eight yards and a half, and the height five cubits or nearly three yards. Keil sets out the front's division into two shoulders of fifteen cubits with three pillars each, and a doorway of twenty cubits between them with four pillars, curtained in the same material as the entrance to the dwelling. Ellicott closes with the orientation and forestalls an objection to it: both tabernacle and temple faced east, which Orientals generally regarded as the front of the world, a belief probably connected with the sun's rising — but, he insists, quite separate from sun-worship.
16:
The gate hanging is agreed to have been the richest thing in the enclosure, and the point of that is drawn out by Ellicott. The word and the description are the same, word for word, as those used of the covering at the entrance to the dwelling; and the coloured needlework would contrast strongly with the plain white sail-cloth round the rest of the court, so that it clearly pointed out to everyone where the way in lay. Clarke reaches the same identification by way of the materials and workmanship, matching them to the inner covering of the tabernacle and to both veils. Gill says simply that this hanging was better than the rest, much finer and richer.

Gill alone asks why the silver fillets are mentioned again after they have already been specified. His answer is a point about the drafting rather than the object: the earlier statement had covered only the pillars of the south and north sides, so the clause is added here to bring in those at the east and west ends. Ellicott repeats his correction of the term itself, that filleted with silver should be united by silver rods.

Ellicott makes one observation about the height that carries beyond this verse. Five cubits, he notes, has not previously been either stated or implied for the court; and he adds that all the measurements of the tabernacle and the court, as distinct from the furniture, are five cubits or a multiple of five, with a single exception — the length of the inner covering, which was fixed by the pitch of the roof.

What the brass vessels were is the one real dispute here, and the two answers turn on different arguments from the metal. Keil is decided: they are not the things required for the performance of worship at all, but the tools used in setting up the tabernacle and taking it down again. Gill offers both possibilities and lands with Keil for a reason he spells out — hammers and the like, as Jarchi and Ben Gersom observe, since the vessels actually used in the sanctuary were of gold or silver or plated with them, and not of brass. Clarke takes the other option, reading them as the instruments used about the altar, and justifies the humbler metal from wear rather than from rank: it would have been improper to use the more precious metals there, since they must soon have been worn out by the severity of the service. Keil, turning from the fittings to the plan, traces the court surrounding the dwelling on all four sides to the same cause that required the dwelling itself to be divided in two, namely that the nation, being unholy, could not come directly into the presence of Jehovah.
20:
Whether the lamps burned by day as well as by night is the live question, and each side cites the same text. Henry, with Wesley following him, has the priests cause the lamp to burn always, night and day. Ellicott restricts it to every night without intermission, reports Josephus for three lights kept burning day and night, and answers that nothing in Scripture confirms it — adding that the tabernacle had light enough by day through the linen entrance curtain, which might also be looped up, and that the evening lighting is asserted in one passage and the morning extinction implied in another. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by the same route, reporting Josephus more fully — all seven burning through the night, four put out in the morning, three kept alight through the day — and setting against it the words about the lamp of God going out in the temple where Samuel lay.

What beaten oil was they agree about and describe differently. Clarke calls it the mother drop, which runs out of itself as soon as the olives are a little broken, and cites Columella — a legitimate evidence, he says, in such matters — for the finer flavour of oil that flows spontaneously or under little pressure. Keil adds only that the olives were cleansed of leaves, twigs and dust before beating. Ellicott notes that the requirement is newly particular, oil having been asked for before but not pure beaten olive oil, and distinguishes the beaten product from what is crushed out in a mill.

On what the oil signifies the readings run parallel rather than against each other. Henry and Wesley make the pure oil the gifts and graces of the Spirit, communicated to believers from Christ the good olive of whose fulness we receive; Henry adds the maintenance of ministers, since the people provided it, and an epigram — that candlesticks without candles are as wells without water or clouds without rain. Both make the tending of the lamps the work of ministers, who by preaching and expounding the scriptures enlighten the church, so that the lamps of the word are lighted as duly as the incense of prayer is offered. Calvin fastens on the purity rather than the substance: since divine illumination was the truth of the symbol, God required oil neither muddy nor mixed with lees, any fault in it detracting from the dignity of the mystery; its purity showed that nothing mean or common was signified, the Israelites being meant to bring pure minds with them. On the perpetual burning he is sharper still, that nothing is more opposed to the worship of God than obscurity, and that it is not enough to be enlightened by puffs, the Spirit's direction being meant to shine from heaven in a perpetual flow. Clarke observes that the temple of Vesta, where a fire was kept perpetually burning, seems to have been formed on this model.

The title tabernacle of the congregation Gill finds nobody has explained. The two usual reasons are that Israel gathered there and that God met Moses there, and neither will hold: not the first, because the candlestick stood in the holy place, which only priests entered; not the second, because God promised to meet Moses in the most holy place, from between the cherubim. His own answer is that Israel assembled at the door and God met them there, so the whole took its name from that. The others take one or other of the horns he rejects. Keil and Ellicott adopt the meeting with God, Keil noting that the expression is applied to the sanctuary here for the first time and suits a structure that was a tent in style; Clarke adopts the assembly, making it the place where all the people were to worship and toward which, as their king's habitation, they were ever to turn in adoration.
